notes:
I found plenty of traditional verse-by-verse comment on Psalm 147. I found very little on the other two parts of your request:

- **Protestant disagreements:** I found no real split between traditions. What shows up is a difference in method. John Gill (Baptist) reads many verses as being about Christ or the church. Calvin (Reformed) and Wesley (Methodist) stay with the plain sense, and in the passages I found Wesley agrees with the older commentators. On v. 9 the sources disagree about a story about ravens (see there).
- **Other views:** For Catholic and Orthodox readings I found only Augustine's sermon on newadvent.org. I didn't reach any netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com or oca.org pages on this psalm. No source mentioned prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace use of it.
- **Verse numbers:** The newadvent.org page labels its quotations "Psalm 146:…", the Latin numbering, but they are this psalm's verses. I've filed them under the BSB verse numbers.

**Background**
- **Date:** Pulpit and Constable link the psalm to Nehemiah's dedication of the city wall. Constable thinks it was likely written for the celebration after Nehemiah and his people finished rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem and resettling the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/147-4.html
- Matthew Henry disagrees. Because it is so much like Psalm 145, he thinks David wrote it, and that vv. 2 and 13 refer to the first building of Jerusalem in David's time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_147.cfm
- **Shape:** The last five psalms have no title in the Hebrew text, and each begins and ends with Hallelujah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- **A scholarly note:** The Expositor's Bible (Maclaren) thinks the stress on God at work in nature is partly an argument against the idol worship Israel met in Babylon, and partly a result of a wider view of God's relation to the world that the Exile brought. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik says "Praise the LORD" both declares praise and encourages it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Spurgeon calls praise good because it is right, acceptable to God, good for us and an encouragement to others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-1.htm
- **Scholarly note:** Some scholars, such as Hupfeld, change one letter so that "good" and "pleasant" describe God, not praise. Maclaren rejects this because calling God "pleasant" is not normal usage, and the usual reading makes good sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Praise must be matched by how we live. Augustine tells his hearers that the tongue praises only for a while, so their whole life should praise. He says God listens to the heart and the life, not the mouth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik reads this as God's care for Jerusalem, perhaps meaning its rebuilding after the exile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Maclaren notes the verb forms may show continuing action: God is always building up Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- Gill (Baptist) allows the literal reading. He also reads it spiritually as the church, which Christ builds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/147.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Jerusalem is the eternal city in heaven. Sin drove humanity out of it, and Christ gathered the scattered back by his blood. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: Israel in exile was broken-hearted, and going home "healed" them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-3.htm
- Spurgeon says hearts break in ten thousand ways, and Christ is good at healing every kind of heartbreak. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Gill links the verse to Christ the physician. In his reading, the broken are hearts broken by the word, with true sorrow for sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-3.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The "bruised" are the humble and the unbruised are the proud. God binds the wounds through the sacraments, the preached word and the church's work, much as a doctor applies bandages. These come off once the soul is fully healed in the heavenly Jerusalem. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 4**
- Maclaren says "counting a number for the stars" means deciding how many there will be, not just counting them. Calling them by name means summoning them, like a captain reading the roll of his troops. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- Pulpit: nothing escapes God's knowledge, and he knew the number and names of the exiles as he knows the stars. https://biblehub.com/psalms/147-4.htm
- Kidner (quoted by Guzik): the verse reverses the familiar argument that our small affairs are too tiny for so great a God to notice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The stars are faithful lights in the church. God counts everyone who will reign with him and leaves out the unworthy, so believers should rejoice that their names are written in heaven. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 5**
- Maclaren says the verse comes from Isaiah 40. The stars have a number, though it is beyond human counting, but God's wisdom has no measure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- Gill (Baptist) takes "Our Lord" to be our Lord Jesus Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-147.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The one who numbers the stars cannot himself be numbered. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik compares it to "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble" (Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Henry: God casts down the proud sometimes by humbling events in this life, and at the latest on the day of everlasting shame. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_147.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Because the verse contrasts them with the gentle, the "sinners" here are the fierce, those who are not gentle. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 7**
- Benson (Methodist): the Hebrew literally reads "answer to the Lord in praise", which may mean singing back and forth, as was the ancient practice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms.html
- Gill, following the Jewish commentator Kimchi, says the first line means singing with the voice and the next line means music on instruments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/147.htm

**v. 8**
- VanGemeren (quoted by Guzik) contrasts the God of Israel with Baal. He says Baal's supposed powers over rain and fertility "were nothing in comparison!" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Henry: dull clouds bring rain, and in the same way clouds of hardship bring showers that make the soul yield the fruit of righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/147.htm
- Gill also reads the clouds as possibly picturing ministers of the word, full of the rain of gospel teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-8.htm
- **Text note:** The Cambridge Bible notes that the Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) add a line from Psalm 104:14, which appears in the Prayer Book Psalter as "and herb for the use of men." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Poole and Wesley (Methodist) say the ravens are named because they were despised and unclean to the Jews, and because their parents abandon them as soon as they can fly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/147-9.html
- **Disagreement about the raven story:**
  - Calvin (Reformed) calls the abandonment story a Jewish fable. For him it is enough that not even the young ravens go without food when they cry out their need. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/147-9.html
  - The Cambridge Bible cites a source that denies there is any basis for the idea that ravens turn out their young too early. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-9.htm
  - Spurgeon's Treasury quotes a writer who says "no bird is more careful of its young ones than the raven." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-147.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached a sermon on this verse, "The Ravens' Cry". If God hears ravens, he will hear a sinner's prayer. And when such a person cries for mercy, it is God the Holy Spirit crying in them. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons12/sermons12.v.html
- **Text note:** Gill says the Greek, Latin and other old versions translate it "that call upon him". He adds that the early church fathers took the ravens as the Gentiles, and their young as Christians descended from them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-9.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott questions the common view that the horse and legs mean cavalry and infantry. He says Eastern nations treated speed of foot as the mark of a strong warrior. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-10.htm
- Pulpit: the denial is relative, not absolute. God values these gifts less than character, not at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-10.htm
- The Geneva Bible notes say using lawful means pleases God, but trusting in them robs God of his honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-10.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: the word here is *hesed*, God's great love, especially his loyalty to his promises and covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Henry: Fear must keep hope from growing into presumption, and hope must keep fear from sinking into despair. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_147.cfm
- Gill adds a Calvinist point. Fear and hope are not the cause of God's delight in his people, which began before the world was made. They only mark out the people God delights in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-11.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: the earlier calls to praise are general, but this one is aimed at Jerusalem, because it has just received special mercies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-12.htm
- Gill reads Jerusalem and Zion here as the spiritual Jerusalem, the Gospel church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-12.htm

**v. 13**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says this refers to Nehemiah rebuilding the walls and setting up the gates (Nehemiah 7:1-3). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/147-9.html
- Spurgeon applies it to the church: he wishes churches were kept safe in the same way from false doctrine and unholy living. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-12.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: "finest wheat" literally means "the fat of wheat", plenty of good-quality wheat. It points to the prosperity of Nehemiah's time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/147.htm
- Gill also reads the wheat spiritually as the Gospel, and especially as Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/147.htm

**v. 15**
- Maclaren: God's word is pictured as a swift messenger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): a word that runs this fast can overtake even those running away from it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Gill gives three readings:
  - the Targum's "Memra", the Word, which he takes to be the Messiah;
  - God's word of providence;
  - or rather the word of the Gospel, perhaps pointing to the apostles' mission.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-15.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** "He sends forth His Word to the earth" is read as God not abandoning fallen people. The Word came to earth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: snow is rare in Palestine but does fall. The hoarfrost-and-ashes comparison was probably picked because the two Hebrew words, kephor and kaepher, sound alike. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/147.htm
- The Biblical Illustrator: snow is said to warm the earth, protecting young plants like a garment of down. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-147.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Snow stands for human nature fallen to earth as love grows cold. "But in that snow are predestined sons of God." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: "morsels" may mean "crumbs", thrown in plenty the way people feed birds, and the ice seems to be hail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/147.htm
- Spurgeon: no one can withstand the extremes of cold any more than great heat. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps147.cfm

**v. 18**
- Henry: the thawing word may picture the gospel and the thawing wind the Spirit of Christ (John 3:8), both sent to melt frozen souls. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_147.cfm
- Maclaren asks whether the God who changes the earth will also breathe on frozen lives and hearts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- Guzik links it to Hebrews 1:3: even snow melting and water flowing happen as God sends out his word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-147/
- Spurgeon's Treasury: in captivity Israel had been icebound, until God sent the spring breeze of his love and they were set free. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps147.cfm

**v. 19**
- Keil & Delitzsch: from the Hebrew verb form, the poet has prophecy in mind as well as the Law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/147-18.htm
- Pulpit: above all physical blessings are the gifts of spiritual light and guidance. https://biblehub.com/psalms/147-19.htm
- Henry: it is a great mercy for any people to have God's word among them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_147.cfm

**v. 20**
- Maclaren: the psalmist is glad that Israel has these gifts, not that other nations lack them. Its privilege is its responsibility. "To glory in privilege is sin; to learn that it means responsibility is wisdom." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/147.htm
- Gill: for many hundreds of years only the Jewish nation had God's revealed word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/147-20.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** What was revealed only to Israel is how the righteous are freed by the grace of God, not by their own merits. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801147.htm
